label: Chapter 5: Neutrality, Iron and a New Dynasty, 1867 to 1914

units.text: The treaty of 1867 promised that the fortress of Luxembourg would be taken apart, and it kept its word.
Over the next sixteen years, work crews tore down the walls, filled in ditches, and blew up forts and bastions.
It was one of the biggest demolition projects in Europe, and when it was done, the city that had been a cramped military stronghold for centuries was suddenly free to grow.
The city took the opportunity.
The land where the defenses had stood became parks, boulevards, and building plots.
New districts spread across the plateau.
The deep valleys that had been military obstacles became green spaces.
And in 1903, the city opened a magnificent stone bridge, the Adolphe Bridge, which sweeps across the Pétrusse valley in two graceful arches.
At the time, it was one of the largest stone arch bridges in the world.
Not everything was destroyed. Parts of the casemates survived, and the old town on its cliffs remained.
In 1994, UNESCO recognized the old quarters and the surviving fortifications of Luxembourg City as a World Heritage site.
The Gibraltar of the North had become, in the end, a beautiful ruin.
With the fortress gone, Luxembourg was now a neutral country.
That sounds peaceful, but it was also a gamble.
The great powers had guaranteed its neutrality together, which in practice meant that if anyone broke it, there was no single power obliged to punish them.
And the country had almost no army to defend itself, only a small corps of volunteers and gendarmes.
Luxembourg's safety depended entirely on the goodwill of its neighbors.
But while the diplomats worried, something else was happening underground, something that would change the country more than any treaty.
In the south of Luxembourg, running down into the neighboring French region of Lorraine, lies a belt of iron ore.
It is called minette, a reddish-brown stone.
For centuries, local blacksmiths had known it was there, but it was almost useless, because it contained a lot of phosphorus, which made the iron brittle and impossible to turn into good steel.
Then, in 1878, two Englishmen, Sidney Gilchrist Thomas and his cousin Percy Gilchrist, developed a method for removing phosphorus from iron.
Suddenly, the poor ore of Luxembourg and Lorraine could be made into excellent steel.
What followed was an industrial revolution in miniature.
Blast furnaces went up along the Alzette and in the southwest corner of the country.
Villages like Esch, Differdange, Dudelange and Rumelange swelled into industrial towns.
Mines opened up in the red hills.
The sky above the south turned orange at night and the dust settled red on everything.
Within a generation, the country that had been exporting its farmers to America was importing workers.
They came from Germany, and then from Italy.
Italian laborers began arriving in large numbers in the 1890s, and they settled in the steel towns, and they would be the first of many waves of immigrants who would reshape the country.
Luxembourg had a tradition of sending its sons and daughters abroad.
Now, for the first time, it began to receive people from elsewhere.
In 1911, the main steel producers merged into a single giant company called ARBED, a name made from the French words for the united steelworks of Burbach, Eich and Dudelange.
For most of the twentieth century, ARBED was practically a state within the state.
By the eve of the First World War, steel was the backbone of the economy, and per head of population, few places in the world made more of it.
The shy farming country had become an industrial power.

The politics of these years were stable, even dull, and the person who embodied that stability was a man named Paul Eyschen, who was head of the government from 1888 until 1915, an extraordinary twenty-seven years.
He was a careful, pragmatic lawyer who guided the country through industrialization and the swirling pressures of its neighbors.
Now we reach one of the most unusual episodes in the whole story: the change of dynasty.
In 1890, King William the Third of the Netherlands died.
He had been both King of the Netherlands and Grand Duke of Luxembourg for forty-one years.
But he had no surviving sons, only a ten-year-old daughter, Wilhelmina.
She became Queen of the Netherlands.
But in Luxembourg, an old family law, the Nassau family pact, said that only men could inherit.
So the Grand Duchy and the Netherlands, united for seventy-five years, separated.
The crown of Luxembourg passed to a distant cousin, a man named Adolphe, the former Duke of Nassau.
His own duchy in Germany had been swallowed up by Prussia in 1866, and he had been living in exile.
Now, in 1890, at the age of seventy-three, he found himself the Grand Duke of Luxembourg.
For the first time, the country had a ruler who lived there, whose family belonged to it, and who was not the king of someone else.
It was the beginning of the modern Luxembourg monarchy.
Adolphe reigned until 1905. His son William the Fourth followed, but he too had a problem: he had no sons, only daughters.
So parliament changed the succession rules in 1907 to allow women to inherit the throne.
When William died in 1912, his eldest daughter, Marie-Adélaïde, became Grand Duchess at the age of eighteen.
The first woman to rule Luxembourg in her own right was a teenager.
In the same years, the little country was producing a few remarkable people who made their mark abroad.
In 1879, a boy named Edward Steichen was born in the village of Bivange.
His family emigrated to the United States when he was a toddler, and he grew up to become one of the greatest photographers of the twentieth century.
In 1955, he organized a legendary exhibition called The Family of Man, which toured the world, and which is permanently displayed today in a castle in the northern Luxembourg town of Clervaux.
Another Luxembourger, the physicist Gabriel Lippmann, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1908 for a method of reproducing colors in photographs.

And a man named Hugo Gernsback, born in Luxembourg City in 1884, moved to the United States in 1904, where he published some of the first magazines devoted to what he called scientifiction, now known as science fiction.
The Hugo Awards, one of the most famous prizes in the genre, are named after him.
All these stories, of mines and bridges, of princesses and physicists, show a small country that had figured out how to punch above its weight.
By 1914, Luxembourg was prosperous, stable, proud, and increasingly sure of its own identity.
It had a language that its writers loved, a dynasty that was its own, and an economy that was growing fast.
But the country still had the same geography, wedged between France, Belgium and Germany.
And the guarantee of the great powers was only as strong as their promises.
In the summer of 1914, a crisis in the Balkans pushed Europe toward catastrophe, and the neutrality of Luxembourg was about to be tested.
